title: Why You Shouldn't Try To Convince Difficult Students To Behave udents-to-behave/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that pulling difficult students aside for private lectures, pep talks, or persuasive appeals backfires because it reveals how much their behavior affects the teacher emotionally, handing over leverage in the relationship. He describes this as a form of human nature: any crack in a teacher's leadership presence invites students to fill it or seize control. Instead of trying to convince students to behave, Linsin recommends following the classroom management plan calmly and matter-of-factly, delivering consequences without emotional investment and walking away as though nothing happened. He does encourage direct, honest praise when real improvement occurs, offering sample phrases teachers can use. The broader message is that steady, day-after-day kindness, consistency, and pleasantness build more influence than persuasion ever could, and that refusing to plead or cajole communicates genuine belief in a student's ability to improve.
points: Trying to convince difficult students to behave reveals how much their behavior affects you emotionally, weakening your leverage.
Any crack in a teacher's leadership presence is one students will instinctively fill or exploit, often unconsciously.
Enforcing consequences calmly and matter-of-factly, without lingering conversation, preserves authority better than persuasion does.
Genuine, direct praise for real improvement should still be delivered honestly and specifically when it's earned.
Refusing to plead, coax, or manipulate communicates a deeper belief in the student's ability to succeed than words alone can.
quotes: But in every case, the teacher is trying to convince the student to behave.
Because, when you try to convince students to behave, you’re showing how much it means to you.
You weaken your influence. You’re cede the upper hand in the relationship and give your most challenging students the power to make or break your day.
When there is a crack in the foundation of leadership, however small, your students will fill it—or wrest control of the classroom right out of your hands.
Deliver your news, then turn on your heal and walk away as if nothing happened. Never let them see you sweat.
Your refusal to pull them aside to woo, plead, coax, cajole, or manipulate communicates loud and clear that you believe in them.
Be the leader they need, not the weak-kneed groveler they don’t.
